sentences.text: Hesperornis was a large bird measuring between 1.5 and 2 meters in length, with some individuals reaching up to 1.8 meters.
This animal had virtually no wings and relied on its powerful hind legs to swim.
The best-known species, Hesperornis regalis, is the only one known from a complete skull.
Dozens of specimens ranging from fragments to nearly complete skeletons have been found in the Smoky Hill Chalk Member of the Niobrara Formation.
Many modern representations inaccurately depict the animal with a beak covering the entire jaw.
Hesperornis rossicus was about 1.4 meters long, making it the largest species of Hesperornis and one of the largest hesperornithines.
Hesperornis was one of the first prehistoric birds identified by science.
The genus Hesperornis was described and established by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1872.
The first species described in the genus was the type species Hesperornis regalis, discovered in Kansas during Marsh's second expedition to the West.
Marsh named the initial discovery Hesperornis regalis, meaning "regal western bird" or "royal western bird".
Marsh later named the smaller species Hesperornis gracilis in 1876 based on an incomplete metatarsus found in the same Niobrara chalk layers.
The diet of Hesperornis consisted mainly of fish and other aquatic creatures.
Studies of limb proportions and hip structure confirm that Hesperornis moved in a manner similar to modern loons or grebes.
Hesperornis were likely excellent foot-propelled divers but probably moved ungainly on land.
Hesperornis legs were likely encased in the body wall up to the ankle, preventing them from standing or walking normally.
Young specimens of Hesperornis grew rapidly and continuously, like modern birds.
Hesperornis belongs to the family Hesperornithidae.
Hesperornis is classified within the class Reptilia.
Species within the genus include H. regalis, H. crassipes, H. gracilis, H. altus, H. montana, H. rossicus, and several species described by Martin and Lim in 2002.
Hesperornis lived from the Coniacian to the Maastrichtian, between 89.8 and 66 million years ago.
Fossils of Hesperornis date to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, with possible records from the early Maastrichtian.
Hesperornis lived in North America from Kansas to Canada within an inland sea, as well as in the waters of the Turgai Strait near Siberia.
Hesperornis was primarily a marine bird that lived in epicontinental seas like the Western Interior Seaway, the Turgai Strait, and the North Sea.
Youngest specimens found in the freshwater Foremost Formation suggest that some Hesperornis species may have partially abandoned their primarily marine habitat for inland waters.
Recent studies question whether Hesperornis had lobed or webbed toes, with both interpretations considered equally likely.
